claim: Research on brain plasticity in deafness consistently emphasizes the reorganization of the auditory cortex.
source: Research on brain plasticity, particularly in the context of deafness, consistently emphasizes the reorganization of the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deaf individuals show remarkable differentiation in functional connectivity from the auditory cortex compared to hearing individuals.
source: Our findings demonstrate remarkable differentiation between individuals deriving from the absence of shared auditory experiences, resulting in heightened FC variability among deaf individuals, compared to more consistent FC in the hearing group.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Connectivity to language regions becomes more diverse across individuals with deafness.
source: Notably, connectivity to language regions becomes more diverse across individuals with deafness.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1A and 1B showing increased variability in language regions.

claim: Increased connectivity diversity in deafness is found in deaf native signers who are exposed to natural language since birth.
source: This does not stem from delayed language acquisition; it is found in deaf native signers, who are exposed to natural language since birth.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis comparing native signing deaf individuals to hearing individuals shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Language experience impacts individual differences in functional connectivity, although to a more moderate extent than hearing loss.
source: However, comparing FC diversity between deaf native signers and deaf delayed signers, who were deprived of language in early development, we show that language experience also impacts individual differences, although to a more moderate extent.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison between native and delayed signers shown in Figure 3.

claim: Deafness induces neural reorganization.
source: Extensive research into neural plasticity in congenital deafness has shown that deafness induces neural reorganization (e.g. Allen et al., 2013; Almeida et al., 2015; Almeida et al., 2018; Amaral et al., 2016; Finney et al., 2003; Lomber et al., 2010; Ruttorf et al., 2023; Scott et al., 2014; for a review, see Alencar et al., 2019; Lomber et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The auditory cortex in deafness becomes highly responsive to visual stimuli.
source: For instance, the auditory cortex (AC) in deafness becomes highly responsive to visual stimuli, reflecting a compensatory adaptation to sensory loss (e.g. Codina et al., 2017; Hauthal et al., 2013; Simon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating visual responses in the auditory cortex of deaf individuals.

claim: The reorganization of the auditory cortex in deaf individuals plays a role in language processing, responding to sign language.
source: Importantly, the reorganization of the AC in deaf individuals also plays a role in language processing, responding to sign language, which uses the visual rather than the auditory modality (Nishimura et al., 1999; Trumpp and Kiefer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research showing auditory cortex responses to sign language.

claim: Visual processing in the auditory cortex in congenital deafness is caused by hearing loss, as opposed to using sign language.
source: Although most findings in congenital deafness that suggest visual processing in the AC are caused by hearing loss, as opposed to using sign language (Cardin et al., 2013; Cardin et al., 2016; Fine et al., 2005), sign language itself also affects cross-modal plasticity, e.g., in the processing of motion (Bavelier et al., 2001; Codina et al., 2017; McCullough et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research distinguishing the effects of hearing loss from sign language use.

claim: Sign language affects cross-modal plasticity in the processing of motion.
source: Although most findings in congenital deafness that suggest visual processing in the AC are caused by hearing loss, as opposed to using sign language (Cardin et al., 2013; Cardin et al., 2016; Fine et al., 2005), sign language itself also affects cross-modal plasticity, e.g., in the processing of motion (Bavelier et al., 2001; Codina et al., 2017; McCullough et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on sign language and motion processing.

claim: People who were congenitally blind have significantly more individual differences in brain connectivity from their deprived visual cortex compared to sighted controls.
source: In this study, we showed that people who were congenitally blind have significantly more individual differences in brain connectivity from their deprived visual cortex beyond what is found in sighted controls. This was especially true in areas where connectivity is reshaped by blindness (Sen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on blindness.

claim: Plasticity may be more variable among people than previously thought.
source: This suggests that plasticity may be more variable among people than previously thought.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings on blindness cited in the manuscript.

claim: Postnatal experience plays a role in driving individual differences in brain development.
source: Further, it illustrates the role of postnatal experience, in driving individual differences in brain development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings on blindness and the current study.

claim: Deaf children born to hearing parents who are raised without direct contact to other deaf adults often suffer from delayed language acquisition.
source: Deaf children born to hearing parents who are raised without direct contact to other deaf adults often suffer from delayed language acquisition as they cannot perceive spoken or sign language in their environment (Hall, 2017; Mayberry et al., 2002; Mayberry and Eichen, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on language acquisition in deaf children.

claim: Early-onset language deprivation has unique effects on brain organization.
source: This early-onset deprivation has unique effects on brain organization as well (Cheng et al., 2023; Lyness et al., 2013; Twomey et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on the effects of language deprivation.

claim: In congenital hearing loss, cochlear implants should be applied in younger rather than older children, as the efficacy decreases if implemented later.
source: In congenital hearing loss, cochlear implants should be applied in younger rather than older children, as the efficacy of cochlear implants decreases if implemented later (Karltorp et al., 2020; Kral and Sharma, 2012; Lyness et al., 2013; Purcell et al., 2021; Sharma and Campbell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on cochlear implant efficacy.

claim: The level of metabolism in the cortex of children prior to cochlear implantation predicted their speech perception outcomes.
source: However, even then, the success of their application might be dependent on the level of the reorganization of the AC: an early work showed that in children prior to cochlear implantation, the level of metabolism in their cortex, including the AC, predicted their speech perception outcomes (Lee et al., 2001), suggesting a challenge posed by reorganization to intact sensory restoration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on cochlear implant outcomes.

claim: Recruitment of the broad auditory cortex for visual speech in deaf adults positively correlates with auditory speech perception following cochlear implantation.
source: In contrast, more recently, it was shown that recruitment of the broad AC (including language areas) for visual speech in deaf adults positively correlates with auditory speech perception following implantation (Anderson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on cochlear implant outcomes.

claim: Multiple regions showed significant intersubject variability differences in functional connectivity from the auditory cortex between the deaf and hearing groups.
source: We found that multiple regions showed significant intersubject variability differences in FC between the deaf and hearing groups (Figure 1A; see also Supplementary file 1, table S1 for the peaks of this effect).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1, table S1.

claim: Regions showing significant intersubject variability differences in functional connectivity include areas of the left temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus and middle temporal gyrus, including the auditory association cortex), the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (including Broca's area), paracentral lobe, and a small part of the dorsal visual cortex.
source: These included areas of the left temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus [STG] and middle temporal gyrus [MTG], including the auditory association cortex), the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (IFG, including Broca's area), paracentral lobe, and a small part of the dorsal visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The clusters in the STG, MTG, and IFG fall, to a great extent, within classically identified language regions.
source: The clusters in the STG, MTG, and IFG fall, to a great extent, within classically identified language regions (see white outline in Figure 1A; mapping language areas from Fedorenko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A and citation to prior research on language regions.

claim: AC-FC had a much more substantial change in variability due to deafness compared to multiple control regions.
source: This major effect of deafness on individual differences in FC was uniquely strong for the AC. Replicating this analysis with multiple control regions (all atlas cortex areas not involved in audition or language; Harvard-Oxford Atlas) showed that AC-FC had a much more substantial change in variability due to deafness (X2=2303.18, p<0.0001; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The deaf show variability over twice as large as the hearing in most of the areas that show change to within-group variability, including the STG, MTG, and the IFG.
source: The deaf show variability over twice as large as the hearing in most of the areas that show change to within-group variability, including the STG, MTG, and the IFG.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The deaf group showed lower variability in only one cluster in the left early visual cortex.
source: The deaf group showed lower variability in only one cluster in the left early visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Auditory experience appears to exert a general stabilizing influence on functional connectivity in hearing individuals.
source: Thus, the findings from this analysis indicate that as in vision, in hearing individuals auditory experience appears to exert a general stabilizing influence on FC, whereas hearing loss leads to greater overall variability between individuals in the connectivity of the AC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing deaf and hearing individuals.

claim: Hearing loss leads to greater overall variability between individuals in the connectivity of the auditory cortex.
source: Thus, the findings from this analysis indicate that as in vision, in hearing individuals auditory experience appears to exert a general stabilizing influence on FC, whereas hearing loss leads to greater overall variability between individuals in the connectivity of the AC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing deaf and hearing individuals.

claim: The deaf had more consistent connectivity between their early auditory and visual cortices.
source: A single exception is that the deaf had more consistent connectivity between their early auditory and visual cortices.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Individual differences dramatically increase due to deafness.
source: This suggests that as in vision loss (Sen et al., 2022), individual differences dramatically increase due to deafness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison to prior research on blindness.

claim: Comparing native deaf signers to hearing individuals revealed increased variability in temporal, frontal, and medial regions.
source: Our results demonstrated a very similar pattern to the one described above, revealing increased variability in temporal, frontal, and medial regions (Figure 1C; see also Table S1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Table S1.

claim: FC variability is higher in the native signing deaf individuals when compared to the hearing individuals.
source: The FC variability is higher in the native signing deaf individuals when compared to the hearing individuals (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Deafness-related factors, even without delayed language acquisition, are sufficient to generate more diverse functional connectivity from the auditory cortex between individuals.
source: This outcome suggests that deafness-related factors, even without delayed language acquisition, are sufficient to generate more diverse FC from the AC between individuals and that auditory experience, regardless of language exposure, exerts a broad stabilizing effect on FC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing native signing deaf and hearing individuals.

claim: Auditory experience, regardless of language exposure, exerts a broad stabilizing effect on functional connectivity.
source: This outcome suggests that deafness-related factors, even without delayed language acquisition, are sufficient to generate more diverse FC from the AC between individuals and that auditory experience, regardless of language exposure, exerts a broad stabilizing effect on FC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing native signing deaf and hearing individuals.

claim: Deaf individuals showed increased functional connectivity to the auditory cortex in frontal, temporal, and parietal regions.
source: Consistent with prior research (e.g. Andin and Holmer, 2022; Ding et al., 2016), deaf individuals showed increased FC to the AC in frontal, temporal, and parietal regions, while for the hearing the connectivity was stronger to sensorimotor areas (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior research.

claim: For hearing individuals, connectivity to the auditory cortex was stronger to sensorimotor areas.
source: Consistent with prior research (e.g. Andin and Holmer, 2022; Ding et al., 2016), deaf individuals showed increased FC to the AC in frontal, temporal, and parietal regions, while for the hearing the connectivity was stronger to sensorimotor areas (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior research.

claim: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between the spatial pattern of variability difference and the spatial pattern of the group effect in terms of AC-FC was modest but highly significant (r=0.24, p<0.0001).
source: The Pearson's correlation coefficient between these two maps was modest but highly significant (r=0.24, p<0.0001 for both smoothed and unsmoothed permuted data; confirmed through a permutation test shuffling voxel location across 100,000 iterations; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a moderate link between variability and plasticity in the auditory cortex.
source: This suggests a moderate link between variability and plasticity: not only is the AC-FC more variable in the deaf, but the variability seems to also be increased in areas that showed reorganization because of deafness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis between variability and reorganization.

claim: All the areas that showed changes to functional connectivity exhibited either greater variability within the deaf group or similar variability in both groups.
source: We found that all the areas that showed changes to FC exhibited either greater variability within the deaf group (mainly in the parietal and right frontal cortex) or similar variability in both groups (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No region showed higher variability in the hearing group among areas that showed changes to functional connectivity.
source: No region showed higher variability in the hearing.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Plasticity functional connectivity of the auditory cortex in deafness is overall linked to more variable outcomes across individuals.
source: Together, this suggests that plasticity FC of the AC in deafness is overall linked to more variable outcomes across individuals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on variability and reorganization.

claim: Comparing deaf native signers to deaf delayed signers identified significant differences in four small clusters: left posterior middle frontal gyrus, left posterior supramarginal gyrus, left dorsal visual cortex (precuneus and cuneus), and the right anterior inferior frontal gyrus.
source: To address this, we replicated the FC variability analysis by comparing deaf native signers to deaf delayed signers, equating hearing loss. In contrast to the results above, which revealed extensive variability change across multiple brain regions, this analysis only identified significant differences between native and delayed deaf signers in four small clusters (Figure 3A; see also Table S1) in the left posterior middle frontal gyrus (pMFG), close to the precentral gyrus (PreCG), the left posterior supramarginal gyrus (pSMG), left dorsal visual cortex (precuneus and cuneus), and the right anterior inferior frontal gyrus (aIFG).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Table S1.

claim: FC variability was increased for the deaf delayed signing individuals both in the left MFG and the right aIFG.
source: FC variability was increased for the deaf delayed signing individuals both in the left MFG and the right aIFG (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The deaf native signing individuals showed higher variability in the pSMG and the dorsal stream (precuneus and cuneus).
source: In contrast, the deaf native signing individuals showed higher variability in the pSMG and the dorsal stream (precuneus and cuneus) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The two areas that had increased variability in delayed signers closely corresponded to language-related areas (pMFG and aIFG).
source: Interestingly, the two areas that had increased variability in delayed signers closely corresponded to language-related areas (e.g. pMFG and aIFG).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and knowledge of language-related brain regions.

claim: Beyond the broader effects of deafness on individual differences in the functional connectivity of the early auditory cortex, delayed language acquisition can also affect individual differences, albeit to a lesser extent.
source: These findings indicate that beyond the broader effects of deafness on individual differences in the FC of the early AC, delayed language acquisition can also affect individual differences, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing native and delayed signing deaf individuals.

claim: AC-FC to different brain regions, primarily in the occipital lobe, but also in posterior MTG, are influenced by the age at which deaf participants began using hearing aids.
source: At the whole-brain level, we observed that AC-FC to different brain regions, primarily in the occipital lobe, but also in posterior MTG (Appendix 1—figure 2), are influenced by the age at which our deaf participants began using hearing aids, such that higher FC is correlated with older ages of onset.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Higher functional connectivity is correlated with older ages of onset of hearing aid use.
source: At the whole-brain level, we observed that AC-FC to different brain regions, primarily in the occipital lobe, but also in posterior MTG (Appendix 1—figure 2), are influenced by the age at which our deaf participants began using hearing aids, such that higher FC is correlated with older ages of onset.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: There was no correlation between the duration of hearing aid use and AC-FC with any brain region.
source: Interestingly, there was no correlation between the duration of hearing aid use and AC-FC with any brain region (no significant clusters, p<0.05, cluster-corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data analysis.

claim: AC-FC to the left fusiform gyrus is correlated with the hearing threshold of deaf participants.
source: We found that AC-FC to the left fusiform gyrus is correlated with the hearing threshold of deaf participants (Appendix 1—figure 2), indicating that more profound hearing loss is associated with stronger FC between the AC and the fusiform gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: More profound hearing loss is associated with stronger functional connectivity between the auditory cortex and the fusiform gyrus.
source: We found that AC-FC to the left fusiform gyrus is correlated with the hearing threshold of deaf participants (Appendix 1—figure 2), indicating that more profound hearing loss is associated with stronger FC between the AC and the fusiform gyrus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: No significant correlations were found between hearing-related parameters (hearing threshold, age of hearing aid use, duration of hearing aid use) and AC-FC to regions showing increased variability in deafness.
source: We performed the same correlation analysis at the region of interest (ROI) level using individual clusters extracted from the map in Figure 1A. No significant correlations were found for any of the factors or ROIs (all p>0.05 before correction for multiple comparisons, see Appendix 1—figures 3-5 for scatterplots of AC-FC and each individual factor).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figures 3-5.

claim: Hearing experience factors such as hearing threshold and age of hearing aid use can influence AC-FC, but they do not account for the observed increased variability.
source: These findings suggest that while hearing experience factors such as hearing threshold and age of hearing aid use can influence AC-FC, they do not account for the observed increased variability observed in our study, underscoring the role of congenital deafness in increasing AC-FC individual differences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on hearing-related parameters.

claim: Congenital deafness plays a role in increasing AC-FC individual differences.
source: These findings suggest that while hearing experience factors such as hearing threshold and age of hearing aid use can influence AC-FC, they do not account for the observed increased variability observed in our study, underscoring the role of congenital deafness in increasing AC-FC individual differences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Individuals in the deaf group display a greater degree of individual variability in their functional connectivity from the auditory cortex compared to a hearing group.
source: This study demonstrates a link between neural plasticity and variability in the AC of deaf individuals. Our study has demonstrated that, in comparison to a hearing group, individuals in the deaf group display a greater degree of individual variability in their FC from the AC.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The increased variability in functional connectivity from the auditory cortex in deaf individuals was not driven by differences in their hearing threshold or hearing aid use experience, but rather by congenital auditory loss.
source: These were not driven by differences in their hearing threshold or hearing aid use experience, but rather by congenital auditory loss.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on hearing-related parameters.

claim: There is a mild relationship between heightened variability and the adaptive changes occurring within the deprived auditory cortex.
source: Furthermore, there is a mild relationship between this heightened variability and the adaptive changes occurring within the deprived AC.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis between variability and reorganization.

claim: The spatial patterns of plasticity and increased individual differences are significantly correlated.
source: Specifically, we found that overall, the spatial patterns of plasticity and increased individual differences are significantly correlated, and there is increased variability in many areas functionally connected to the AC that have undergone reorganization due to deafness.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is increased variability in many areas functionally connected to the auditory cortex that have undergone reorganization due to deafness.
source: Specifically, we found that overall, the spatial patterns of plasticity and increased individual differences are significantly correlated, and there is increased variability in many areas functionally connected to the AC that have undergone reorganization due to deafness.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Some increased variability was found when comparing deaf individuals who had varying degrees of sign language acquisition.
source: Further, some, although more modest, increased variability was found when comparing deaf individuals who had varying degrees of sign language acquisition, suggesting that language acquisition timing itself also plays an additional significant role in producing different AC functional connections.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Language acquisition timing plays an additional significant role in producing different auditory cortex functional connections.
source: Further, some, although more modest, increased variability was found when comparing deaf individuals who had varying degrees of sign language acquisition, suggesting that language acquisition timing itself also plays an additional significant role in producing different AC functional connections.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing native and delayed signing deaf individuals.

claim: Hearing loss in itself may be sufficient to increase individual differences.
source: These findings suggest that although hearing loss in itself may be sufficient to increase individual differences, the variation of the FC patterns in the AC in response to deafness can increase further when considering a combination of auditory experience and timing of language acquisition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The variation of the functional connectivity patterns in the auditory cortex in response to deafness can increase further when considering a combination of auditory experience and timing of language acquisition.
source: These findings suggest that although hearing loss in itself may be sufficient to increase individual differences, the variation of the FC patterns in the AC in response to deafness can increase further when considering a combination of auditory experience and timing of language acquisition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The interaction of auditory and language exposure may amplify the spectrum of functional connectivity diversity from the auditory cortex.
source: Together, these findings show how the interaction of auditory and language exposure may amplify the spectrum of FC diversity from the AC, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex factors shaping neural plasticity in response to deafness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The auditory system undergoes a critical phase during which its organization is fine-tuned by sensory experience.
source: The auditory system, like the visual system, undergoes a critical phase during which its organization is fine-tuned by sensory experience (Knudsen, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hearing loss leads to significant reorganization of the auditory cortex.
source: Given the fundamental role of auditory input for the AC organization, hearing loss leads to significant reorganization of this brain region.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: The extent of reorganization of the auditory cortex may vary among individuals with deafness.
source: Importantly, while hearing loss induces cross-modal plasticity in the AC, we show that the extent of reorganization may vary among individuals with deafness.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: The absence of visual experience increases individual differences in brain connectivity in blindness.
source: Recent evidence on blindness (Sen et al., 2022) suggests that the absence of visual experience increases individual differences in brain connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Hearing loss influences the neural connectivity profile of the deprived auditory cortex, introducing variability in the network outcomes.
source: Our findings demonstrate how hearing loss influences the neural connectivity profile of the deprived AC, introducing variability in the network outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Much of the increased individual differences are found in areas that belong to the language system, including Broca's area and the left STG and MTG.
source: Much of the increased individual differences are found in areas that belong to the language system, including Broca's area (notably bilaterally) and the left STG and MTG (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Deafness can impact top-down connectivity in the auditory cortex.
source: It also aligns with animal studies showing how deafness can impact top-down connectivity (Yusuf et al., 2020) and cortico-cortical interactions (Yusuf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Deafness can impact cortico-cortical interactions in the auditory cortex.
source: It also aligns with animal studies showing how deafness can impact top-down connectivity (Yusuf et al., 2020) and cortico-cortical interactions (Yusuf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Connectivity between the early auditory cortex and many language regions is stabilized or affected by the use of audition for language in early life and becomes less consistent in its absence.
source: Therefore, it appears that connectivity between the early AC and many language regions is stabilized or else affected by the use of audition for language in early life and becomes less consistent in its absence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Hearing loss has a potential stabilizing impact on the interaction between the auditory and visual cortices.
source: This suggests a potential stabilizing impact of hearing loss on the interaction between the auditory and visual cortices, possibly due to the prevalent use of vision for adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing lower variability in the visual cortex for the deaf group.

claim: Postnatal sensory experience promotes consistency in brain organization.
source: Overall, these results, coupled with those of Sen et al., 2022, highlight the impact of postnatal sensory experience in promoting consistency in brain organization, suggesting a general principle of brain development of the sensory systems.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison to prior research on blindness.

claim: The exhibited heightened AC-FC variability by the deaf group corresponds spatially to regions that reorganize in deafness.
source: Our finding that the exhibited heightened AC-FC variability by the deaf group corresponds spatially to regions that reorganize in deafness, even if only moderately (r=0.24), suggests that the increased variability may be partly attributed to the reorganization and adaptation of neural circuits in response to hearing loss.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The increased variability may be partly attributed to the reorganization and adaptation of neural circuits in response to hearing loss.
source: Our finding that the exhibited heightened AC-FC variability by the deaf group corresponds spatially to regions that reorganize in deafness, even if only moderately (r=0.24), suggests that the increased variability may be partly attributed to the reorganization and adaptation of neural circuits in response to hearing loss.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: Higher AC-FC variability was found in regions such as the inferior frontal cortex and pre-supplementary motor area.
source: Although not all areas that changed their mean FC to the AC showed increased variability in the deaf group, we found higher AC-FC variability in regions such as the inferior frontal cortex and pre-supplementary motor area.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The inferior frontal cortex and pre-supplementary motor area exhibited functional reorganization in response to deafness.
source: These same brain regions exhibited functional reorganization in response to deafness, as illustrated in Figure 2B, consistent with prior resting-state fMRI research emphasizing functional changes following hearing loss (e.g. Andin and Holmer, 2022; Ding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in the mean connectivity of the auditory cortex likely reflect the change in its function in deafness.
source: Importantly, these changes in the mean connectivity of the AC likely reflect the change in its function in deafness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and prior research.

claim: The auditory cortex can be activated in deaf individuals when performing parallel visual tasks.
source: Studies have shown that the AC can be activated in deaf individuals when performing parallel visual tasks, indicating a shift in functional activation from auditory to visual processing (e.g. Almeida et al., 2015; Benetti et al., 2017; Benetti et al., 2021; Bola et al., 2017; Bottari et al., 2014; Butler et al., 2017; Finney et al., 2001; Lomber et al., 2010; Meredith and Lomber, 2011; Petitto et al., 2016; Scott et al., 2014), albeit typically for the same type of functional computation (Cardin et al., 2020; Heimler et al., 2015; Lomber, 2017; Pascual-Leone and Hamilton, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Functional responses of the auditory cortex may vary across individuals in accordance with their variable levels of functional connectivity alterations.
source: Our results suggest that such functional responses may vary across individuals in accordance with their variable levels of FC alterations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Higher AC-FC variability was found in regions that show a decreased functional connectivity to the temporal lobe in deafness, specifically the somatosensory cortex.
source: Interestingly, in addition to finding increased variability in connectivity for areas that increase their connectivity in deafness, we also found higher AC-FC variability in regions that show a decreased FC to the temporal lobe in deafness, specifically the somatosensory cortex (e.g. Andin and Holmer, 2022; Bonna et al., 2021; Ding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Differences in somatosensory involvement have been identified between deaf and hearing individuals, which has been linked to sign language and visual processing.
source: Here too, previous research has identified differences in somatosensory involvement between deaf and hearing individuals, which has been linked to sign language and visual processing (Bonna et al., 2021; Okada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Any type of plasticity in the connectivity of the auditory cortex, regardless of its direction (increased or decreased FC), may manifest variably across individuals.
source: Therefore, it appears that any type of plasticity in the connectivity of the AC, regardless of its direction (increased or decreased FC), may manifest variably across individuals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Functional recruitment of auditory cortex for nonauditory tasks is supported by evidence from animal studies demonstrating causal links.
source: Although the term 'reorganization' is debated, and some concerns exist about the functionality of neural reorganization (Makin and Krakauer, 2023), functional recruitment of AC for nonauditory tasks is supported by evidence from animal studies demonstrating causal links (Lomber et al., 2010; Meredith and Lomber, 2011; for a review, Alencar et al., 2019; Lomber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Functional changes in the auditory cortex appear to arise from a combination of unmasking and re-weighting of nondominant inputs, rather than extensive anatomical alterations.
source: Such functional changes appear to arise from a combination of unmasking and re-weighting of nondominant inputs, rather than extensive anatomical alterations (Alencar et al., 2019; Kral and Sharma, 2012; Kral and Sharma, 2023; Kupers et al., 2010; Pascual-Leone and Hamilton, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The findings of increased variability in functional connectivity from the auditory cortex in the deaf suggest more than mere unmasking.
source: Our findings of increased variability in FC from the AC in the deaf suggest more than mere unmasking, as this variability cannot easily be explained without assuming some degree of reorganization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Auditory deprivation leads to significant disruptions in the development and maintenance of brain connectivity patterns in congenitally deaf cats and other animal models.
